title: What made Kansas City riffs distinctive
summary: Kansas City riffs always carried a melody you could build a song from, like Moten Swing and Lester Young's riffs.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x:
Well, before we leave Basie, Eddie, I'd like -- you know, it's often been said that the Kansas City style was notable for its use of riffs. But as we both know, the (unintelligible) like Fletcher were using riffs before Basie came East, et cetera, et cetera.

Well, what would you say were the sort of most distinctive things about Kansas City jazz?

Well, the difference in the Kansas City riff and riffs other places out through the world was, the Kansas City riff always carried a melody that you could write a song from. All those riffs can be a song, like Lester Young with '77. That was a riff, but it made a melody. And some Symphony Sid
of the riffs that I heard up East, they didn't make good melodies.
No, they were just sort of like punctuations.

Yeah, I don't know what you'd call it, but the Kansas City riff, you could always write a song from it, like many of the riffs. Moten Swing, that was a riff, just made up for an ensemble to go along with Driving Me Crazy. Then we made a melody out of it.
And that's one of the numbers.
